newsitem.title: USA: Life-ending guidance less common in Germany/Japan.
newsitem.headline: Life-ending guidance less common in Germany/Japan.

text.p: Dialysis patients of one in 20 U.S. kidney specialists dictated in advance when to stop the life-saving treatment, while doctors in Germany and Japan rarely got such guidance, researchers said on Tuesday.

About five percent of U.S. kidney specialists surveyed reported they followed directives submitted by dialysis patients to withdraw treatment when their situation became hopeless. That compared to less than 2 percent of German specialists and less than 1 percent of Japanese doctors.
The reasons for the disparity may be both medical and cultural, according to researchers from MetroHealth Medical Center in Cleveland who surveyed 232 kidney specialists in the three countries.

Dialysis patients in Germany and Japan tend to be younger and have fewer additional diseases than in the United States, where the decision to stop dialysis accounts for one-third of kidney patient deaths, study author Ashwini Seghal wrote in the Journal of the American Medical Association.

The decision to stop dialysis often follows development of additional medical problems or sheer exhaustion. An examination of 155 U.S. cases found that half of the patients were mentally incompetent at the time of withdrawal, pointing up the need for advance directives, Seghal wrote.

Practitioners in Germany and Japan have few legal statutes or court cases governing the end-of-life decision, even though most physicians said they would be willing to follow advance directives in the case of mentally incompetent patients.
In Japan, the emphasis on social relatedness rather than individualism has led physicians and families to make most decisions about medical care even for mentally competent patients.
